blocks.x: The following is a conversation at the Elks Club on March 3rd, 1968 with Elton Purnell, the pianist.
Say something, Elton, just say anything. Hello, folks. Yeah.

On these programs, we try and bring you from time to time somebody of note in the jazz field, and today we have the great pleasure of bringing a friend of ours that I wish we'd known longer than we have. A fellow who plays a very fine piece of piano by the name of Elton Purnell. Elton, I'm glad to have you here.
Glad to be here, too, man.
I got a record of yours that was made in Hamburg with Jimmy Archie and Darnell Howard and the rest. Have you made any since then?
Yeah, we made some records in England, too. We just got them here in America, and I think they were some of the greatest records we made.
Who you got with you on it?
Well, almost the same band, just about the same band. The only difference in the band is that the one in English boy, Keith Smith, is playing trumpet on it.
Those English boys play a mighty fine hunk of jazz sometimes.
Yeah, Keith Smith is very good. He's been out of New Orleans listening to the jazz and learning everything he could, and I think he's really improved. I think it's doing him good.
I'm just wondering, is the record out now?
Yeah, the record's out now. I think Bill Basin has some.

I'll get one from him before we quit. Alton, I've heard a lot of your records going way back, I think. I don't know whether you ever played with Oliver on Snagit, of which I've got a copy at home, but I'm sure you were back in there somewhere.
No, I didn't play with Oliver, but I made Snagit with Bunk Johnson, which is one of the old trumpet players around Oliver's age, you know.

Well, Bunk Johnson, if I remember correctly, the records I've got of his, he made with Lou Waters up at Hambone Kelly some years ago after they rediscovered Bunk. You know, they found him pitching cotton or something. I don't know what he was doing, but they brought him a new set of teeth and brought him a trumpet, and away we went.

Yeah, this is the time, around the time I played him, but we were in New York, but we played in 1945, and we made a lot of records while we were there that were very good records. And it's too bad, I mean, Bunk had to pass away, you know, because this was my first chance to do any kind of traveling outside of the South by playing along with Bunk. See, Bunk hired the George Lewis band, which we all played together, and he was just a new man in the band. And so when Bunk came in and accepted our band to play with him, then they named it Bunk Johnson's band.
Yeah, boy, it could play an awful lot of instrument, that fella.
Yeah, Bunk was a pretty good old man.
When did he die, Oden?
Oh, five years ago, was it? Well, no, it was longer than that. Bunk died in the 50s, or maybe in the 40s. I don't know, around 50s, late 40s or 50s.
I think it was in the 50s, because I know I was at a station in Berkeley at the time when he passed on, and it was an awful shock to all of us because he was a great fella.
Yeah, he was a fine guy. I liked the way he played. He was so different from the rest of those other trumpet players. Musically, he used to make all these runs on the diminished chords, you know?
Uh-huh. Mm-hmm. I know also that he used to talk down by, he sang down by the riverside on one record, and he always talked about laying your weapons instead of your weapons down.
Yeah, well, Bunk comes from a new-eyed bearing that these people pronounce their words a little different from other people, you know.
I know, but it's distinctly Bunk.
Yeah, that's Bunk.
Getting back to you for a minute, what are your prospects for the future here?
Well, I'm expecting to go to England in the next three or four months. I'm waiting on a letter to go to, I guess, around England, France, and Germany and a couple of places around Europe.
You're going to be one of our American ambassadors abroad, I suspect.
It seems that way. I've been over there about five or six times, and I'm pretty well-known, you know.
How do they accept Dixieland over in Europe?
Oh, they're really crazy about it in Europe. They're really crazy about it.

I mean, I know Satch has done an awful lot over there, but I just wondered how you other fellows that are not, if you pardon me, I'm not belittling you, but you're not as known to the public in general as well as Satch is.

No, I don't think I am, but I'm very well-known all around the world. I've been playing all around Australia and Sweden, Switzerland, and all like that, and I'm very well-known around the world, but not as good as Satch.

Well, no, I wasn't belittling you, because I've known you for a good many years. I mean, I've known your technique and your ability and your records and so forth, and I've got a lot of them home, and I play them too. But I have to admit, and I think you will too, that as far as publicity goes, I think Satch has a little more than you have.
Oh, yes, Satch is the greatest, man. That's my best friend.

I haven't seen him in years. I had him on interviews some years ago when he had Tee Garden with him and Barrett Deems and a lot of the other boys were with him at the time. They were playing over in San Francisco, and we had him on the air, and he was a kick to talk to.
Oh, I could just talk to Louis, but I don't have to hear him play. Just talk with him, and I enjoy myself. He's a wonderful guy to talk with, man, you know.
Alton, do you find that Louis sings about the way he plays?

Yeah, he does sing about the way he plays, you know. He's got a wonderful mind, man. He makes some of the stuff, all the stuff that he does on his trumpet is really new, man. You know, he's got wonderful ideas. He should be an arranger.
Well, I think he probably does that as he goes along all the time. He's busy arranging things from time to time.
Yeah, well... Well, all you fellows do.
I mean, you never play the same thing twice the same way.

Most of the original jazz men from down in New Orleans always play that way, you know. It's hard to explain how these things come from your mind into your fingers or the way you play them, but they all fit in, you know.

Well, Alton, I'm going to let you go because I got a record here with you on it, and I'd like to play it, and we're going to tell the people about it. But I think this is a very good example of a very fine pianist who's been doing a tremendous job for a good many years, and I won't tell you how old he is. He looks much younger, I'm sure, than he feels sometimes playing these sessions. But, Alton Pernell, thanks very much for being with us, and we'll see you again soon, maybe?
Thank you. Glad to be here. Yeah, you'll see me again.
Okay, thanks, Alton. Bye-bye.
